source_text: Quoniam de immortalitate animae diximus, sequitur ut doceamus quatenus homini et quando tribuatur, ut in hoc quoque prauitatis ac stultitiae suae perspiciant errores qui mortales quosdam decretis placitisque mortalium deos esse factos opinantur, uel quod artes inuenerant uel quod usum I quarundam frugum docuerant uel quod utilia uitae hominum , prodiderant uel quod inmanes bestias interemerant. quae, merita quam longe ab inmortalitate semota sint, et docuimus in prioribus libris et nunc docebimus, ut appareat solam esse iustitiam quae uitam homini pariat aeternam, et solum deum qui aeternae uitae praemium largiatur. nam illi qui suis meritis inmortales facti esse dicuntur, quia nec iustitia nec ulla in his uera uirtus fuit, non inmortalitatem sibi, sed mortem\' peccatis ac libidinibus quaesierunt neque caeleste praemium, sed inferna supplicia meruerunt, quae pendent simul cum iis omnibus qui eos coluerunt. cuius iudicii propinquare tempus ostendam, ut et iustis merces digna soluatur et poena merita inpiis inrogetur. Plato et multi alii philosophorum cum ignorarent originem rerum supremumque illut tempus quo mundus esset effectus, multa milia saeculorum fluxisse dixerunt, ex quo hic pulcherrimus mundi extiterit ornatus, secuti fortasse Chaldaeos, qui, ut Cicero tradit in libro de diuinatione primo, quadringenta septuaginta milia annorum monumentis conprehensa se habere delirant: in quo se quia posse argui non putabant, liberum sibi crediderunt esse mentiri. nos autem, quos diuinae litterae ad scientiam ueritatis erudiunt, principium mundi, finemque cognouimus: de quo nunc in fine operis disseremus, quoniam de principio in secundo libro explicauimus. sciant igitur philosophi qui ab exordio mundi saeculorum milia enumerant, nondum sextum millesimum annum esse conclusum. quo numero expleto consummationem fieri necesse est et humanarum rerum statum in melius reformari: cuius rei argumentum prius enarrandum est, quo ratio eluceat. Mundum deus et hoc rerum naturae admirabile opus, sicut arcanis sacrae scripturae continetur, sex dierum spatio consummauit diemque septimum, quo ab operibus suis requieuerat, sanxit. hic est autem dies sabbati, qui lingua Hebraeorum a numero nomen accepit, unde septenarius numerus legitimus ac plenus est. nam et dies septem sunt quibus per uicem reuolutis orbes conficiuntur annorum et septem stellae quae non occidunt et septem sidera quae uocantur errantia, quorum dispares cursus et inaequabiles motus rerum ac temporum uarietates efficere creduntur. ergo quoniam sex diebus cuncta dei opera perfecta sunt, per saecula sex id est annorum sex milia manere in hoc statu mundum necesse est. dies enim magnus dei mille annorum circulo terminatur, sicut indicat propheta, qui dicit: ante oculos tuos, domine, mille anni tamquam dies unus. et sicut deus sex illos dies in tantis rebus fabricandis laborauit, ita et religio eius et ueritas in his sex milibus annorum laboret necesse est, malitia praeualente atque dominante. et rursus quoniam perfectis operibus requieuit die septimo eumque benedixit, necesse est ut in fine sexti millesimi anni malitia omnis aboleatur e terra et regnet per annos mille iustitia sitque tranquillitas et requies a laboribus quos mundus iam diu perfert. uerum quatenus id eueniat, ordine suo explicabo. saepe diximus minora et exigua magnorum figuras et praemonstrationes esse, ut hunc diem nostrum, qui ortu solis occasuque finitur, diei magni speciem gerere, quem circuitus annorum mille determinat. eodem modo etiam figuratio terreni hominis caelestis populi praeferebat in posterum fictionem. nam sicut perfectis omnibus quae in usum hominis molitus est deus ipsum hominem sexto die ultimum fecit eumque induxit in hunc mundum tamquam in domum iam diligenter instructam, ita nunc sexto die magno uerus homo uerbo dei fingitur, id est sanctus populus doctrina et praeceptis dei ad iustitiam figuratur. et sicut tunc mortalis atque inperfectus e terra fictus est, ut mille annis in hoc mundo uiueret, ita nunc ex hoc terrestri saeculo perfectus homo fingitur, ut uiuificatus a deo in hoc eodem mundo per annos mille dominetur. quomodo autem consummatio futura sit et qualis exitus humanis rebus inpendeat, si quis diuinas litteras fuerit scrutatus, inueniet. sed et saecularium prophetarum congruentes cum caelestibus uoces finem rerum et occasum post breue tempus adnuntiant describentes quasi fatigati et dilabentis mundi ultimam senectutem. quae uero a prophetis et uatibus futura esse dicantur, priusquam superueniat extrema illa conclusio, collecta ex omnibus et coaceruata subnectam.
pass_a_gloss: Since we have spoken about the immortality of the soul, it follows that we teach to what extent and when it is granted to man, so that in this also the errors of their perversity and foolishness may be perceived by those who think that certain mortals have been made gods by the decrees and decisions of mortals, either because they discovered arts or because they taught the use of certain fruits or because they handed over useful things for the life of men or because they killed savage beasts. Which merits, how far they are removed from immortality, we have taught in the previous books and now we will teach, so that it may appear that only justice is what gives eternal life to man, and only God who grants the reward of eternal life. For those who are said to have been made immortals by their own merits, because neither justice nor any true virtue was in them, they did not seek immortality for themselves, but death by sins and lusts, and they did not merit the heavenly reward, but the infernal punishments, which hang together with all those who worshiped them. I will show that the time of this judgment is approaching, so that a worthy reward may be paid to the just and a deserved punishment may be inflicted on the impious. Plato and many other philosophers, since they were ignorant of the origin of things and the supreme time when the world was made, said that many thousands of years had passed since this most beautiful ornament of the world existed, perhaps following the Chaldeans, who, as Cicero hands down in the first book on divination, are delirious, having comprehended 470,000 years in their records: in which they, because they did not think they could be accused, believed it was free for them to lie. But we, whom the divine letters teach to the knowledge of truth, know the beginning and the end of the world: about which we will now discuss at the end of the work, since we explained the beginning in the second book. Therefore, let the philosophers who enumerate thousands of years from the beginning of the world know that the sixth thousandth year has not yet been completed. When this number is fulfilled, it is necessary that the consummation be made and the state of human things be reformed for the better: the argument of which thing must be explained first, so that the reason may shine forth. The world, this admirable work of the nature of things, God, as it is contained in the secrets of the sacred scripture, completed in the space of six days, and sanctified the seventh day, on which he rested from his works. This is the day of the Sabbath, which in the Hebrew language has its name from the number, from which the septenary number is legitimate and full. For there are seven days by which the orbits are completed in turn, and seven stars that do not set, and seven planets that are called wandering, whose unequal courses and motions are believed to produce the varieties of things and times. Therefore, since all the works of God were perfected in six days, it is necessary that the world remain in this state for six thousand years, that is, six centuries. For the great day of God is terminated by a circle of a thousand years, as the prophet indicates, who says: before your eyes, Lord, a thousand years are like one day. And just as God labored in those six days in making so many things, so also his religion and truth must labor in these six thousand years, with malice prevailing and dominating. And again, since he rested on the seventh day after completing his works and blessed it, it is necessary that at the end of the sixth thousandth year all malice be abolished from the earth and justice reign for a thousand years, and there be tranquility and rest from the labors that the world has been suffering for a long time. But how this will happen, I will explain in order. We have often said that smaller and insignificant things are figures and premonitions of greater things, so that this our day, which is finished by the rising and setting of the sun, bears the image of the great day, which is determined by a circuit of a thousand years. In the same way, the figure of the earthly man also prefaced the fiction of the heavenly people. For just as God, after completing all things that he had made for the use of man, made man himself on the sixth day, and led him into this world as into a house already carefully prepared, so now on the sixth great day the true man is fashioned by the word of God, that is, the holy people are formed by the doctrine and precepts of God to justice. And just as then the mortal and imperfect man was made from the earth, so that he might live for a thousand years in this world, so now the perfect man is fashioned from this earthly age, so that, vivified by God, he may dominate in this same world for a thousand years. However, how the future consummation will be and what kind of exit human things have in store, if someone has scrutinized the divine letters, he will find. But also the voices of secular prophets, congruent with the heavenly ones, announce the end of things and the downfall after a short time, describing as if the final old age of a tired and decaying world. What the prophets and seers say will happen before that final conclusion comes, I will collect and add from all things.

pass_b_english: Since we have spoken of the soul's immortality, we must now teach to what extent and when that gift is granted to humanity, so that those who imagine certain mortals were made gods by mortal decrees and judgments may see their own perversity and folly exposed here as well — whether because they discovered arts, taught the use of certain crops, bestowed useful gifts for human life, or slaughtered savage beasts. How far such merits fall short of immortality we have shown in the earlier books and will show again now, so that it becomes clear that justice alone begets eternal life for man, and God alone bestows the reward of eternal life. For those who are said to have become immortals by their own merits — since neither justice nor any true virtue dwelt in them — did not win immortality for themselves, but death through sins and lusts; they earned not a heavenly reward but infernal punishments, which hang over them and over all who worshiped them. I will demonstrate that the time of this judgment is drawing near, so that a worthy recompense may be paid to the just and a deserved penalty inflicted on the impious.

Plato and many other philosophers, ignorant of the origin of things and of the supreme moment when the world was made, declared that many thousands of ages had elapsed since this most beautiful ordering of the world came into being — perhaps following the Chaldeans, who, as Cicero reports in the first book of On Divination, delude themselves by claiming to possess records embracing 470,000 years. Because they thought they could never be called to account, they believed themselves free to lie. But we, whom the divine scriptures instruct in the knowledge of truth, know both the beginning and the end of the world. We will now treat the end at the close of this work, since we explained the beginning in the second book. Let the philosophers who count thousands of ages from the world's beginning understand that the sixth millennium has not yet run its course. When that number is complete, the consummation must come and the condition of human affairs be reformed for the better. The argument for this must be set forth first, so that the reason may shine forth.

God completed this admirable work of nature, the world, in the space of six days, as the secrets of sacred scripture contain it, and hallowed the seventh day on which he rested from his labors. This is the Sabbath day, which in Hebrew takes its name from the number, and from this the number seven is legitimate and full. There are seven days by which the orbits are completed in their turn, seven stars that never set, and seven planets called wandering, whose unequal courses and motions are believed to produce the varieties of things and times. Therefore, since all God's works were perfected in six days, the world must remain in this present state for six ages — that is, six thousand years. For the great day of God is bounded by a circle of a thousand years, as the prophet declares: "Before your eyes, Lord, a thousand years are like one day" (Psalm 90:4). And just as God labored during those six days in fashioning so many things, so his religion and truth must labor through these six thousand years while malice prevails and dominates. And again, because he rested on the seventh day after perfecting his works and blessed it, at the close of the sixth millennium all malice must be abolished from the earth, and justice must reign for a thousand years, with tranquility and rest from the labors the world has long endured. How this will come to pass I will explain in due order.

We have often said that lesser and fleeting things are figures and foreshadowings of greater things, so that this present day of ours — bounded by the sun's rising and setting — bears the image of the great day, which is determined by a circuit of a thousand years. In the same way the figure of the earthly man prefigured the formation of the heavenly people. For just as God, after completing all things made for man's use, fashioned man himself on the sixth day and led him into this world as into a house already carefully prepared, so now on the sixth great day the true man is fashioned by the Word of God — that is, the holy people are formed by God's doctrine and precepts unto righteousness. And just as then a mortal and imperfect man was formed from the earth to live a thousand years in this world, so now the perfect man is fashioned from this earthly age, that, vivified by God, he may rule in this same world for a thousand years. But how the future consummation will be, and what outcome awaits human affairs, anyone who searches the divine letters will discover. The voices of secular prophets, harmonious with the heavenly ones, also announce the end of things and the downfall after a brief time, describing as it were the final old age of a weary and decaying world. Whatever the prophets and seers declare will happen before that final consummation arrives, I will gather from all sources and link together.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. Scripture citation (Psalm 90:4) correctly identifies the allusion 'ante oculos tuos, domine, mille anni tamquam dies unus'.
